Mission

Beyond GDP

There is an international debate about framing climate change in policy beyond GDP — judging what a changing climate does to lives, not only to output. DigiÉire takes that framing seriously and makes it operational for one country and one hazard.

Ireland’s position in the North Atlantic places it under the direct influence of ocean circulation and weather systems that redistribute heat and moisture around the planet. Its extensive coastline and settlements along estuaries make rising seas a particular threat, connecting changes in the global ocean and the loss of distant glaciers and ice sheets to the wellbeing of communities at home.

The setting is not subtle. Global mean temperature reached +1.53 °C above the 1951–1980 baseline in 2024, the warmest year in the instrumental record, because fossil CO2 emissions were still climbing — 38.6 billion tonnes that year. Thermal expansion and the loss of glaciers and ice sheets have already put global mean sea level about 218 mm higher than it stood in 1900. Recorded flood disasters worldwide have gone from about 26 a year in the 1970s to 171 a year across 2015–2024.

On top of that trend sits El Niño, which redistributes heat and rainfall across the Pacific every few years and shifts storm tracks well beyond it. It modulates the signal rather than producing it: the strong events of 1997–98 and 2015–16 stand out as spikes on a line that was already rising.

Ireland receives all of this as local weather. It is small enough to model as a whole and coastal almost everywhere, with towns and cities built along estuaries that already flood. Sea-level rise will not arrive as a single event; it will arrive as more frequent bad days in places people have lived for generations.

A cost-benefit sheet handles damage to buildings well and damage to people badly. The worry before a storm, the months in temporary accommodation, the insurance that will not renew, the sense of being unheard by the bodies meant to help — these are the durable costs of flooding, and they are the ones this project measures.

What should we adapt for, if not for how well people are able to live?

  • Coastal communities first — where exposure is highest
  • To 2100 — the horizon adaptation decisions actually reach
  • Wellbeing as the quantity maximised, not damage avoided
